sections.body: Rare disease diagnosis covers the use of AI to shorten the diagnostic odyssey for patients with conditions that individually affect few people but collectively are common. It spans phenotype capture, genomic variant prioritization, literature and database search, and reanalysis of previously unsolved cases. Among the 1000 medical AI models tracked on this site, rare disease diagnosis is a small but growing category, often overlapping with pediatric genetics and undiagnosed disease programs. The work is not a single test but a pipeline that combines clinical features, family history, sequencing data, and curated knowledge.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The infrastructure includes short and long read sequencers, secure compute for genomic data, and reference resources such as ClinVar, OMIM, HPO, and gnomAD. AI components typically run on GPUs or cloud instances, with pipelines orchestrated by workflow languages and containers. Tools such as Exomiser and phenotype driven search engines are common in research and clinical settings, though deployment varies by lab. Data storage and transfer must meet privacy rules, so many programs use institutional clusters or compliant cloud environments.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method usually starts with structured phenotype terms, then aligns them with candidate genes and variants using similarity scores or machine learning rankers. Variant calling from sequencing reads is followed by filtering, annotation, and prioritization, with AI used to weigh evidence from population frequency, predicted impact, inheritance, and literature. Some systems use facial analysis or text mining to suggest diagnoses, but these outputs are treated as hypotheses for clinical review. Reanalysis of negative cases is a core activity because new gene disease associations appear over time.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance covers patient consent, data privacy, and the provenance of reference data and model versions. Rare disease data is identifiable even when de-identified, so access controls, audit trails, and data use agreements are standard. The site tracks 219 compliance and regulation pages, reflecting the dense rules around genetic information, diagnostic claims, and software as a medical device. Liability risk includes missed diagnoses, false positives, and reliance on outdated databases, so documentation of model inputs and limitations matters.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward integrating multi omics, long read sequencing, and international data sharing to solve more cases. AI models are likely to become better at handling incomplete phenotypes and diverse ancestries, though validation in real clinical settings remains a bottleneck. Reanalysis pipelines may become continuous rather than one time, and patient facing summaries may help families understand results. The main open questions are evidence standards, reimbursement, and how to keep knowledge current without overloading clinical teams.
